name: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
title: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
answer: Threat modelling for legal AI is the structured practice of identifying, prioritising, and mitigating threats to AI systems used in legal work, including legal research, drafting, contract review, e-discovery, and matter management. It covers threats to confidentiality, attorney-client privilege, work product, client data, and the integrity of legal outputs, such as prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction, unauthorized access, and manipulated or hallucinated results. The scope extends beyond the model to the surrounding workflow, including retrieval, orchestration, human review, and the third-party tools that feed the system. Because legal AI often handles sensitive material, the threat model must account for both security failures and professional responsibility obligations. The site tracks 732 AI tools, which reflects the breadth of components that can enter a legal AI stack and therefore the breadth of the threat surface.

It covers threats to confidentiality, attorney-client privilege, work product, client data, and the integrity of legal outputs, such as prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction, unauthorized access, and manipulated or hallucinated results. The scope extends beyond the model to the surrounding workflow, including retrieval, orchestration, human review, and the third-party tools that feed the system. The site tracks 732 AI tools, which reflects the breadth of components that can enter a legal AI stack and therefore the breadth of the threat surface.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Legal AI typically runs on cloud infrastructure, private data centres, or a hybrid of both, with foundation models accessed through APIs or deployed as open-weight models behind enterprise controls. Supporting components include vector databases for retrieval, document management and e-discovery platforms, identity and access management, encryption and key management, logging and monitoring, and orchestration layers that connect models to legal workflows. Threat modelling must map these components, the data flows between them, and the trust boundaries where client data, privileged material, or model weights could be exposed. Many legal AI tools are delivered as software as a service, so responsibility for security is shared between the vendor and the law firm or legal department.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI follows established methods such as data flow diagrams, trust boundary analysis, STRIDE, LINDDUN, MITRE ATLAS, attack trees, and abuse case development, adapted to legal contexts. A typical exercise brings together security, legal, data science, and compliance staff to map assets, enumerate threats, rate likelihood and impact, and define controls. Legal-specific threats include privilege leakage through prompts or logs, hallucinated citations that reach a filing, bias in risk scoring, unauthorized practice of law, and discovery sanctions. Teams test controls with red teaming, prompt injection exercises, retrieval evaluation, and output monitoring, then document the model and review it as the system changes. The site tracks 29 AI case law precedents, which can inform how courts treat these risks and therefore how threat models should be scoped.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in legal AI threat modelling centre on attorney-client privilege, work product, confidentiality, data protection, intellectual property, and professional responsibility rules. Provenance matters because legal teams must know where training data, model weights, prompts, and outputs came from, who licensed them, and what audit trails exist. Risk management includes bias assessment, human oversight, vendor due diligence, contractual protections, and incident response for leaks or harmful outputs. The site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, 6979 state AI bills, 148 active AI lawsuits with 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, all of which shape the obligations a threat model must reflect. This is a description of practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI is moving toward continuous, automated assessment that is integrated with model operations, procurement, and legal service delivery. Expected developments include wider use of standards such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001, more scrutiny of provenance and privilege in audits, and threat models that cover agentic systems and multi-model pipelines. The site's tracking of 6979 state AI bills and 148 active AI lawsuits suggests that regulatory and litigation pressure will keep changing the risk landscape. Legal AI vendors and enterprise legal teams are likely to see threat modelling become a routine part of vendor review and internal controls. The field will need to balance innovation with defensible documentation, human oversight, and clear accountability.
